proxy_language: Mycenaean Greek (Linear B), with Classical Greek (Attic/Ionic) as a secondary attested source for general lexicon
proxy_rationale: 'The Mountain Court' is a fictional later court in the Greece/Aegean/Anatolian coast region with no named historical language. The best-attested language for a Late Bronze/Early Iron Age Aegean palace court is Mycenaean Greek (Linear B tablets, c. 1450-1200 BCE), supplemented by Homeric/Classical Greek vocabulary and the pre-Greek Aegean substrate (e.g. -nth-, -ss- words). Link is medium because the culture is generic, not a specific attested state. Pre-Greek substrate and Anatolian (Luwian/Lydian) coastal names are noted but not used as primary models.
phonology: Mycenaean Greek: vowels a e i o u, with length contrast not marked in Linear B. Stops: voiceless p t k, voiced b d g, labiovelars kw gw (written q-), aspirates largely merged or unmarked. Fricative s; semivowels j (y) and w; liquids r (l/r not distinguished in Linear B, written r-series), nasals m n. Digamma w is retained in Mycenaean (lost in Attic). Pre-consonantal and intervocalic -h- possible, mostly dropped in writing. Diphthongs ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou.
phonotactics: Underlying syllables are (C)V(C) with onsets of single consonants or stop+liquid/nasal and s+stop clusters (e.g. pt-, str-, sk-). Linear B orthography simplifies: CV syllabary, final consonants omitted, clusters broken by dummy vowels. In the Latinized scholarly form, words end in vowels or in -s, -n, -r (nominatives -s, -n, -r, -ō). Typical case endings: nom. -s/-os/-a/-ē/-on, gen. -o(jo)/-ās, dat. -ei/-ai. Stress is not marked. No word-final stops except via dropping in transcription.
orthography: Use the standard scholarly Latin transliteration of Mycenaean Greek: syllabic values joined by hyphens in Linear B transcription (wa-na-ka, pa-si-te-o-i), or normalized Greek forms (wanax). For game names use the normalized unhyphenated form with plain letters: a e i o u p t k b d g q? (avoid) s m n r l? (l only in Classical Greek names) z w j h, and digraphs kh ph th (Classical), ai ei oi au eu ou. Latin-script names avoid c, x (except as ks), f, v, and use k for kappa.
morphology: Highly inflected: nouns in three declensions (thematic -os/-on, -ā/-ē, consonant stems -s, -n, -r, -es), three genders, cases nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative. Verbs mark person, number, tense, voice. Agent nouns in -tēr/-tōr, -eus (profession), -ās; abstract in -sis, -ā, -mos; adjectives in -ios, -ikos, -inos, -eios; diminutives -ion, -iskos. Reduplication in perfects and some nouns. Personal names are common compounds (Eteokles, Alexandros) and divine names (Poseidāwōn, Diwiya).
compounding: Compounds are head-final: first element is a combining stem (often with -o- linker, e.g. hippo-, theo-, andro-), second element the head. Pattern X-o-Y: 'horse-tamer' = hippo-damos. Governing compounds ('Y-maker', 'Y-bearer'): Y-stem + -o- + verbal noun in -os/-ēs (e.g. -phoros 'bearer', -ergos 'worker', -arkhos 'leader'). 'X of Y' is expressed with genitive: head noun + genitive noun (or genitive-head order in names: Diwo-pāter 'father of Zeus'-type patronymics in -idās/-iadēs). Place names often end in -ssos/-nthos (substrate) or -polis, -ai, -ēs, -ōn.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective typically precedes noun (agreeing in case/number/gender) in default order, but may follow; genitive attribute usually follows head noun in prose and inscriptions, precedes in compound names. Demonstratives and articles: Mycenaean has no definite article. Example: wanaka ... 'lord of the ...' with genitive following.

sources: Ventris & Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek (2nd ed. 1973)
Chantraine, Dictionnaire etymologique de la langue grecque (1968-80)
notes: The Mountain Court is not an attested historical state, so the proxy is a regional period language, not a specific court's language. Pre-Greek Aegean substrate (-nth-, -ss-) and Anatolian coastal names (Luwian, Lydian) may be used sparingly for place names but are poorly known and lower-confidence. Current game names like Robi dorux, Xusa cusuta, Cadox use x and c and non-Greek shapes; replace with vowel-final or -s/-n/-r-final forms. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since the language is not Goidelic.
